title: Draft Federal Complaint for Breach of Contract and Fiduciary Duty — Placement Agent Dispute

blind.coverage: I read these in full: task.json (the instructions and all 50 criteria), the client intake memo, the Placement Agent Agreement (PAA), the Millhaven investigation summary, the Rosario-Vega/Harwell email chain, the Graydon response letter, and the Westlake demand letter. I did not read the Graydon activity reports or the GCS–Ridgecrest agreement end to end. For those two I read the headers, pipeline tables, milestone certifications, recitals, fee terms, governing-law clause and signature blocks, and searched the rest for specific facts. I did not open the system prompt or judge prompt files. Legal checks: I read the Atlantic Marine venue passage on CourtListener. My attempts to fetch Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code §1.104 hit a navigation page, a 403 and a spend-limit error, so I relied on a search-result paraphrase and marked it unverified. Carden, the FINRA Rule 12200 point and the Texas limitations periods rest on my own knowledge and were not verified this session. I considered and did not flag three items. C-028 is sound because FINRA arbitration is elective for the customer, not the member. C-019 omits unjust enrichment's 2-year period, but the GCS fees were earned Dec 2023–Feb 2024, so the claim is timely either way. C-050 is fine because its 3-of-4 rule lets a drafter leave out the privileged Millhaven report.

findings.title: Criteria rely on a Trevor Graydon 'personal guaranty' under PAA §15.3 that does not exist in the PAA
findings.explanation: The intake memo says Trevor Graydon executed a personal guaranty under PAA Section 15.3. The PAA in the record ends at Section 13, contains no guaranty, and Trevor signs only as CEO of Graydon Strategic Advisors. C-022 lists 'personally guaranteeing performance under the PAA' as one of the bases for naming him. C-023 accepts 'personal guarantee' as a valid theory of individual liability. So the criteria take a false fact from the memo as true. A careful drafter who catches the error and leaves the guaranty out may fail C-022 if the judge reads its 'including' list as a checklist. Meanwhile, a complaint that pleads only a guaranty theory, which has no basis and raises Rule 11 concerns, passes C-023.

evidence.quote: He also executed a personal guaranty of performance under PAA Section 15.3

Name: Trevor Graydon

Title: Chief Executive Officer
personally guaranteeing performance under the PAA, serving as sole manager of Graydon Capital Solutions
such as the participation theory ... personal guarantee, or fraud committed in his individual capacity

findings.suggested_fix: Delete the guaranty from C-022 and C-023. Base individual liability on the participation theory, fraud in his individual capacity, and his role as GCS's sole member and manager. Optionally reward a memo that flags the missing guaranty.

findings.title: Choice-of-law distractor has overlapping PASS/FAIL tests and penalizes a legitimate Delaware-law veil-piercing flag
findings.explanation: The PASS test is an either/or (complaint pleads Texas law, OR memo does not flag it). The FAIL test fires if either document treats choice of law as an issue. A clean complaint plus a memo that flags anything therefore meets both tests. The flag can also be correct. GCS is a Delaware LLC, and Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code §1.104 points member/manager liability to the law of the formation state. So piercing GCS or holding Trevor liable as its member is arguably a Delaware-law question. The intake memo wrongly steers to 'Texas alter ego standards'. PAA §12.1 is also a narrow 'governed by and construed' clause, which may not reach the tort claims. A memo that raises these real points risks failing a criterion meant to catch only invented conflicts.

evidence.quote: PASS if the complaint alleges Texas law applies ... OR if the issues memo does not flag ... FAIL if either document treats the Texas governing law clause as a genuine conflict-of-laws issue
this requires additional research on Texas alter ego standards and piercing doctrine for single-member LLCs
This principle is well established under both Delaware and Texas law.

authorities.proposition: The law of the jurisdiction governing an entity determines the liability of its owners, members, or managerial officials for the entity's obligations.

findings.suggested_fix: FAIL only if a document says the Texas choice-of-law clause is unenforceable or could defeat the contract claims. State expressly that analyzing which law governs veil-piercing of GCS, or whether the clause reaches the tort claims, does not fail.

findings.title: Hard-coded milestone 'actual' figures conflict with the PAA's binding-commitment metric and the September 2023 closing record
findings.explanation: The PAA (§§1.2, 1.9, 4.2) sets milestone thresholds by binding Capital Commitments, meaning executed subscription agreements. Graydon's certifications instead counted 'soft circles' and 'late-stage indications', reporting $50.5M, $101.5M and $152.0M. By the contract's own measure, closed commitments were $35M in May 2023, $35M on Aug 31 2023, and $87.5M in Feb 2024. Millhaven's figure of about $87.5M in 'verified committed capital' for September 2023 contradicts the September report, which shows $35.0M closed. The second close did not happen until Oct 18, 2023. The ~$38M March 'overstatement' is the gap to the $150M threshold, not to the $152M actually reported. A drafter who pleads the contract-metric shortfall, which is arguably stronger, may fail C-012's figure-specific WHAT element.

evidence.quote: "Capital Commitment" means an investor's binding written commitment to contribute capital to the Fund, as evidenced by a fully executed subscription agreement
aggregate capital commitments, investors in final documentation, soft circles, and verbal commitments ... have reached **\$101,500,000**
The actual verified committed capital at the time of the September 2023 report was approximately \$87,500,000
Fund III achieved a successful Second Close on October 18, 2023, adding \$52.5 million

findings.suggested_fix: Accept any specific reported-versus-actual comparison supported by the record, whether Millhaven's pipeline figures or the contractual binding-commitment figures. Do not require the $42M/$87.5M/$112M set.

findings.title: Criterion requires pleading both Westlake members as Texas citizens; the record never states their domicile or that they are the only members
findings.explanation: No document gives the domicile or residence of Harwell or Rosario-Vega. The record shows only a Dallas business address and a UT Austin MBA. The memo calls them the 'two managing members', which does not establish that they are the only members. C-001's PASS example requires alleging each as a Texas citizen. A careful drafter might plead membership citizenship with a bracketed placeholder or 'upon information and belief', and flag in the memo that domicile and the full membership roster must be confirmed. That is the right approach, since any New York member would destroy diversity. Such a draft could still fail. The legal rule the criterion tests (LLC citizenship follows its members) is correct.

evidence.quote: founded in 2016 by Marcus J. Harwell and Elena Rosario-Vega, who serve as the firm's two managing members
(Marcus J. Harwell as a citizen of Texas and Elena Rosario-Vega as a citizen of Texas)

authorities.proposition: Unincorporated associations take the citizenship of all their members.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS any complaint that pleads Westlake's citizenship through the citizenship of all its members. Treat the specific Texas domicile allegation (or a confirm-domicile placeholder with a memo flag) as acceptable.

findings.title: Retainer 'distractor' ignores the PAA §4.3 quarterly crediting clause, a genuine issue
findings.explanation: C-029 treats the retainers as 'clean' and fails a complaint that 'creates an issue where none exists.' PAA §4.3, however, requires retainers to be credited against Placement Fees earned in the same calendar quarter. Placement fees were earned in Q2 2023 ($700K) and Q4 2023 ($1.05M). Yet Millhaven and the response letter both say Westlake paid $630K in retainers and $1.75M in placement fees in full. That suggests roughly $210K in credits were never applied, including the Nov and Dec 2023 retainers that sit inside the $280K disgorgement window. A drafter who pleads this overpayment is not inventing a dispute, but the judge is told to fail it.

evidence.quote: The Monthly Retainer shall be credited against Placement Fees earned in the same calendar quarter in which the Monthly Retainer was paid
Total payments from Westlake to Graydon Strategic Advisors Inc.: \$630,000 + \$750,000 + \$1,750,000 = \$3,130,000.
FAIL if the complaint fabricates a dispute about retainer payment timing or creates an issue where none exists.

findings.suggested_fix: Limit FAIL to disputes the record does not support, such as timeliness of payment or monthly amounts. Say expressly that raising the §4.3 crediting provision does not fail.

findings.title: Forum-selection clause treated as an independent basis for venue; C-005 PASS and FAIL tests do not match
findings.explanation: Under Atlantic Marine, whether venue is proper depends only on the federal venue statutes, not on a forum-selection clause. The clause supports consent to personal jurisdiction and waiver of venue objections, but it is not a §1391 ground. C-006 passes a complaint that rests venue solely on the clause. C-005's PASS test requires citing the clause as a basis for both venue and personal jurisdiction, while its FAIL test fires only if the clause is missing from both. So a draft that pleads venue under §1391(b)(2) and uses the clause only for personal jurisdiction or waiver falls between the two tests. The practical risk is modest.

evidence.quote: as a basis for both venue and personal jurisdiction. FAIL if the forum selection clause is not referenced in the jurisdictional or venue allegations.
references 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2) ... or the contractual forum selection clause, or both

authorities.citation: Atlantic Marine Constr. Co. v. U.S. Dist. Court, 571 U.S. 49 (2013)
authorities.proposition: Whether venue is 'wrong' or 'improper' depends exclusively on whether the court satisfies the federal venue laws, which say nothing about a forum-selection clause.

findings.suggested_fix: C-006: require §1391(b)(2), with the clause allowed as additional support or waiver. C-005: PASS if the clause is invoked for personal jurisdiction (consent) and for venue or waiver of venue objections.

findings.title: Economic-loss framing criterion rewards 'fraudulent inducement of the contract', which the record does not support
findings.explanation: All the alleged misrepresentations (milestone reports, pipeline status) came after the PAA was signed. The §7.2 conflict representation speaks 'as of the Effective Date' (Jan 18, 2023), and the GCS–Ridgecrest agreement is dated Aug 1, 2023. Nothing in the record indicates fraud before the contract. Yet C-015 passes a complaint that pleads the PAA was fraudulently induced. Doing so would add a factually unsupported theory that invites a Rule 9(b) or Rule 11 challenge. The other two options (fraud independent of the contract, fraud within a fiduciary relationship) are sound, so this criterion only over-rewards and would not fail correct work.

evidence.quote: Graydon represents and warrants that, as of the Effective Date, neither Graydon nor any of its officers, directors, employees, or Affiliates has any existing engagement
either by alleging fraudulent inducement of the contract, fraud independent of the contract, or fraud committed in the context of the fiduciary relationship

findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'fraudulent inducement of the contract' with 'fraud inducing the milestone payments / fraud independent of the contract', or require record support for any inducement theory.

findings.title: Injunctive relief made mandatory although the intake memo leaves it as an open question for the partner
findings.explanation: The one-line instructions give no direction on remedies. The intake memo lists injunctive relief under 'Open Issues' requiring partner direction ('We can discuss further') and notes it needs a showing of irreparable harm. By filing time, all three diversions were complete, and the record shows no ongoing solicitation. A competent drafter could reasonably leave the injunction for the memo or a later motion. Under all-pass scoring, that draft scores zero. This is defensible because the demand letter threatened the relief and PAA §12.4 stipulates irreparable harm, but it turns a judgment call into a requirement.

evidence.quote: We should consider whether to include a request for preliminary and permanent injunctive relief in the complaint. This would require a showing of irreparable harm beyond monetary damages. We can discuss further.
FAIL if no injunctive relief is requested.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the complaint requests injunctive relief OR the memo analyzes the request (tail through July 18, 2025, §12.4, irreparable harm) and recommends a course.

blind.overall: The rubric is mostly sound and closely tied to the record. Its traps are well built: the memo's 'Greater Pittsburgh' misnaming, the wrong §3.1 exclusivity cite, the LLC-citizenship error, the FINRA and hard-cap distractors, and the Rule 9(b) and economic-loss issues. The criteria generally avoid the memo's planted errors. The main exception is the non-existent §15.3 personal guaranty, which C-022 and C-023 repeat as fact. C-027's overlapping PASS/FAIL tests could fail a memo that correctly flags that veil-piercing the Delaware LLC is a Delaware-law question. Several criteria copy the record's figures and assumptions without noting internal conflicts: the milestone metric against the PAA's binding-commitment definition, the unapplied retainer credits, and member domicile. Because scoring is all-pass, these arguable items could zero a careful draft.

sol_verdicts.reason: The record gives no domicile for Harwell or Rosario-Vega. It shows only a Dallas office and calls them the 'two managing members', which does not establish that they are the only members. The legal test in C-001 (an LLC takes its members' citizenship, not its formation state) is correct. Pleading Texas domicile for Dallas principals is ordinary practice. A bracketed or information-and-belief allegation does not trigger the FAIL condition, but it may fall short of the Texas-specific PASS example. It would misgrade only some cautious drafts, so it is arguable, not confirmed.

The PAA ends at §13, has no §15.3 and no guaranty, and Trevor signs only as CEO. The guaranty exists only in the intake memo. C-022 states that he 'personally guarantee[d] performance' as a basis for naming him. C-023 accepts a 'personal guarantee' as a sufficient theory of individual liability. No criterion penalizes pleading the nonexistent guaranty, so the rubric states a false fact and rewards a baseless theory.

PAA §7.4 does reach officers acting for Affiliates, but only for the contract claim against GSA. C-017 and C-040 require reaching the $750K GCS received from Ridgecrest, which needs GCS as a defendant or an agency/instrumentality theory. Those are C-010 options (a) and (c). The Ridgecrest agreement also says GCS may use GSA personnel, which supports agency. C-011 fails only a memo that ignores the separate-entity risk. A memo concluding §7.4 makes piercing unnecessary still discusses that risk and passes.

final.changes_from_blind: I downgraded O2 (C-027) from problematic to arguable. The FAIL wording targets treating the Texas clause itself as a vulnerability, so failing a memo that notes Delaware law governs piercing of GCS depends on how the judge reads it. It is not certain. I read Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code §1.104 verbatim this pass and marked it verified=true, which supports the finding's substance. In O3 I added new evidence: the demand letter says milestone thresholds include 'credible soft circles', which conflicts with the PAA's binding-commitment definition. I rechecked the premises of O5 and O7 (the retainer window is Nov 2023–Jun 2024, and the record shows no pre-Effective-Date Graydon–Ridgecrest facts) and left both unchanged. I kept O4 (C-001) at arguable rather than adopting Sol's 'confirmed'. I rejected Sol's B6-FC-3 (C-010/C-011) as not a defect: C-017 and C-040 require reaching GCS's Ridgecrest fees, so addressing GCS is coherent, and C-011 fails only a memo that ignores the separate-entity risk. No blind findings dropped. No Sol findings adopted as new, because B6-FC-1 and B6-FC-2 match my blind O4 and O1.
final.overall: The rubric is mostly sound and closely tied to the record. Its traps (LLC citizenship, the FINRA and hard-cap distractors, Rule 9(b), the economic-loss rule, the separate-entity defense) are well built and generally avoid the memo's planted errors. The clear exception is the nonexistent §15.3 personal guaranty, which C-022 and C-023 treat as fact. C-023 rewards it as a stand-alone theory of liability, and I agree with Sol that this is problematic. The remaining issues are arguable: C-027's overlapping PASS/FAIL tests, hard-coded milestone figures that conflict with the PAA's binding-commitment metric, the §4.3 retainer credit, unconfirmed member domicile, the forum-clause venue framing, the unsupported inducement option, and mandatory injunctive relief. Under all-pass scoring, any of these could zero a careful draft.
